---

### Changed

- **An invite is a way in, not the key.** Generating an invite used to hand
  over a server's write capability directly — a string that never expires, has
  no limit on how many times it can be used, and cannot be taken back once
  seen. Worse, it worked on a gated server too: `gated` decides who is
  *believed* as a member, not who can *read*, so a screenshot of an invite was
  permanent, unrevocable access to a server's entire history, admitted or not.

  An invite now names where to ask rather than carrying anything to read with.
  Making one asks a server's owner to sign a record — who it admits, and as
  what role, for how long, for how many people, and whether every arrival
  needs a yes or is let straight through — and the string handed over carries
  only a secret checked against that record's hash and the addresses of the
  owner's devices. Redeeming it dials one of those devices, which checks the
  secret, checks the invite hasn't expired or run out or been withdrawn, asks a
  person if the invite says to, and only then mints the real ticket — at the
  same moment it writes the admission, so the two can never come apart. An
  owner can see every invite they've made, how much of it is spent, and pull
  one back with a button that now does something.

  The consequence worth being plain about: an invite needs somebody home. A
  ticket used to work whenever anybody in the server was reachable, because the
  ticket was the whole of what was needed; now a device of the owner's account
  has to answer. Several of an owner's devices are listed as places to ask, so
  one being asleep isn't usually the end of it, but a server run from a single
  laptop that's shut is a server nobody can join until it's open again. That
  trade is the price of the key not being handed out to begin with, and it
  cannot be had both ways.

  What this does not do: make a server's key recallable. Somebody already
  admitted keeps what they were given, the way they always could — this
  changes who ever receives a key and when, not what happens afterward. Private
  channels still turn on their own key rotation for that; a public channel
  stays readable by anyone who was ever let into the server. An invite made by
  an older Ruze, or handed between your own devices while pairing, still works
  exactly as before — this only changes what a fresh invite to a stranger is.
